paras: The lynching of Granville Harrell took place on the night of Saturday, December 18, 1880, when a mob took Harrell, a Black man accused of murdering his employer, from the Hinds County jail at Raymond, Mississippi, and hanged him to a tree outside the town. A coroner's jury found that unknown men had done it and cleared the sheriff and his deputies. Mississippi papers covered both the killing and the lynching at length, while the national wire ran it as a one-line item.

On the morning of Thursday, December 16, 1880, David Simmons, a German-born meat-market owner in West Jackson, was killed with an ax, and Harrell, who had long worked for him, was accused of the killing. The Comet wrote of 'some trouble in regard to their financial affairs' and of a quarrel that morning, but the Weekly Clarion said hardly an unpleasant word had ever passed between the two men. Officer Fitzpatrick arrested Harrell with the ax still in his hands and, according to The Comet, barely got him to jail ahead of a gathering mob. An inquest jury in Jackson found that Simmons died from ax blows dealt by Harrell and called it premeditated murder.
Fearing a lynching, Sheriff Morrison moved Harrell early Thursday night from the Jackson jail to the county jail at Raymond, which papers placed sixteen to eighteen miles away.

On Saturday night a body of men went to the Raymond jail, overpowered the officers, took the keys and brought Harrell out. A wire account printed in Ohio said he locked his arms around a post and that it took fifteen men to pull him loose. He was hanged from a tree near Snake Creek, just outside the town limits, and was found there hanging by the neck. The Weekly Clarion reported that before he died he repeated his confession and implicated other people, whose names it declined to print 'for prudential considerations'.

A coroner's jury met at Raymond on December 19 and found that a mob of 75 to 100 unknown men had taken Harrell from the jail. It cleared the sheriff and his deputies, who it said had been overpowered and forced to give up the keys, and Harrell was buried that Sunday morning on the coroner's orders. No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The Jackson papers gave far more space to Simmons than to Harrell: the Clarion called the killing 'A Cruel and Foul Murder', printed a tribute to Simmons as an upright citizen, and called Harrell 'the fiend'. The Comet had written that money troubles brought out 'the old Satan in the negro', and it headed its report of the lynching 'Swift Retribution'. Raymond's own paper, as quoted in The Comet, noted that the hanging tree stood within yards of spots where mobs had killed Black men in 1862, 1866 and 1875.

The Brookhaven Ledger expected outside criticism and began its report by saying that Northern Republican papers now had 'material for another Southern outrage'. Outside Mississippi the story ran mostly as a single wire sentence in late December, in papers from Maine and Michigan to Minnesota, Arkansas and Missouri. These items said Harrell had 'brutally murdered' Simmons and was lynched by 'a masked party' or 'an armed mob', and many placed the lynching at Jackson rather than Raymond.

Reports of the mob's size ranged from fifty masked men in a Jackson telegram to the New Orleans Picayune, to 75 to 100 in the coroner's verdict, to 150 in the Brookhaven Ledger, which alone said the mob included Black men as well as white. Most accounts date the lynching to Saturday night, December 18, but one Pascagoula paper put it the night after the killing and others gave Sunday or the 19th. The papers also told different stories about what Harrell did after the killing: The Comet said he attacked a lady and a boy, the Clarion said his wife stopped him from striking Simmons's daughter, and the wire version said he only told the daughter where her father's body lay.

reader.title: Lynching of Granville Harrell
bases: A mob took Granville Harrell, a Black prisoner accused of murder, from the Hinds County jail at Raymond and hanged him to a tree (A5, A9, A11).

A mob of between fifty and 150 men overpowered the jail officers, took Harrell from his cell and hanged him without trial (A4, A9, A11). It acted on the accusation that he had murdered David Simmons (A5, A11).

Two Jackson papers, a Jackson telegram to the New Orleans Picayune, the Raymond coroner's verdict and separate wire reports agree that a mob took Harrell from the Raymond jail and hanged him (A5, A9, A11, A14).

accounts.label: Jackson local press
accounts.gist: The Comet and the Weekly Clarion described the ax killing of Simmons in detail. The Clarion reported that the sheriff moved Harrell to Raymond and that a numerous body of unknown persons overpowered the jailer on Saturday night and hanged him after he repeated his confession.

accounts.label: Raymond coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Harrell was taken from the county jail by 75 to 100 unknown men and found hanging near Snake Creek outside Raymond; the sheriff and deputies were overpowered and forced to give up the keys.

accounts.label: Jackson telegram to the New Orleans Picayune
accounts.gist: Fifty masked men overpowered the jailer at Raymond and hanged Harrell to a tree a short distance from the jail.

accounts.label: Brookhaven Ledger
accounts.gist: Friends of Simmons, a mob of 150 'whites and blacks', took Harrell from his cell on Saturday night and hanged him near the town.

accounts.label: National wire
accounts.gist: Short items said a masked party or an armed mob lynched Harrell on the night of the 18th. A longer version said fifteen men were needed to break his grip on a post.

framing.detail: The Comet headed its report 'Swift Retribution' and said Harrell 'fully acknowledged his unmitigated guilt'; the Clarion called him 'the murderer' and 'the fiend'.
Brookhaven Ledger's 'A Murderer Lynched' opened by saying Northern Republican papers now had 'material for another Southern outrage'.
The Comet's 'A Fatal Locality' set the hanging tree in a list of earlier deaths at the spot, including three Black men killed by mobs.
Northern and Midwestern papers ran one-sentence wire items, some describing Harrell as having 'brutally murdered' Simmons.

conflicts.note: The Jackson papers, the inquest dated December 19 and the telegram of the 19th ('last night') all point to Saturday night, December 18.

info: Taken from the Hinds County jail at Raymond and hanged to a tree outside the town's corporate limits, near Snake Creek
Granville Harrell, described as 'a negro' or 'colored' (also spelled Harrel, Harroll)
Accused of killing his employer David Simmons, an elderly white meat-market owner, with an ax on December 16, 1880; a Jackson inquest jury called it premeditated murder, and papers said he confessed
Unknown men; Brookhaven Ledger called them friends of the murdered man and said they were 'whites and blacks'
Buried Sunday morning by direction of the coroner
